title: The shape of Genesis
summary: Eleven times Genesis names the tôlədôt (“generations”, “account”) of the heavens and the earth or of a man. Readers of the book divide it at these verses, but differ over whether each opens the section after it or closes the one before, and some divide the book elsewhere. Three outlines are drawn here on the same verses, in the order they were proposed.

sources.title: ‘The Toledot of the Book of Genesis and Their Redemptive-Historical Significance’
sources.author: Marten H. Woudstra
sources.note: Calvin Theological Journal 5, pp. 184–189

markers.label: “This is the account of …”
markers.summary: Eleven verses name the tôlədôt of the heavens and the earth or of a man: the Hebrew is ʾēlleh tôlədôt (“these are the generations of”), or at 5:1 zeh sēper tôlədôt (“this is the book of the generations of”). The BSB renders the phrase “This is the account of” in ten of them. The word comes twice more in Genesis, in a list (10:32, 25:13), not in this phrase. Esau has two, at 36:1 and 36:9; there is none of Abraham.

This is the account of Jacob

readings.label: Tablets closed by the formula
readings.summary: Wiseman reads the formula as a colophon, the line that closed an ancient tablet and named its writer or owner, so that each one ends the section before it: “It is the concluding sentence of each section, and therefore points backward to a narrative already recorded.” On this reading Moses compiled Genesis from the tablets of the men named.
body: Wiseman argues from what follows the formula: “This is the book of the generations of Adam” tells nothing more of Adam but his age at death, what follows Isaac’s formula is about Jacob and Esau, and there is no formula of Abraham, who would have the best claim to one if it opened a man’s history. He finds that each section ends before the death of the man it names. The chapters after 37:2, mainly of Joseph in Egypt, have “no ending formula”.

He writes that commentators “of all schools of thought”, naming Skinner, Keil and others, “divide the Book into sections which begin with the phrase”, and quotes Driver’s Genesis for that view. Woudstra reports D. J. Wiseman developing the thesis in 1969, and quotes W. H. Gispen’s answer: “This hypothesis is very improbable and does not suffice as an explanation of the toledot formulas.”
readings.note: Wiseman divides 6:9, 11:10, 11:27, 25:19 and 37:2 within the verse, the formula closing one tablet and the rest of the verse opening the next; each is drawn whole with the tablet it closes. He gives the tablets of Ishmael and Isaac, and of Esau and Jacob, as runs, not one by one.

readings.label: Ten sections, each opened by the formula
readings.summary: Holwerda, in lectures at Kampen in 1946, and Külling after him read each formula as the heading of the section that follows, so that Genesis “consists of ten toledoth-sections, each appropriately introduced” by it (Woudstra’s summary). The two of Esau make one section.
body: On Holwerda’s reading, as Woudstra reports it, tôlədôt means what came of someone, and the name after it marks a new starting point: Terah’s section has Abraham at its centre, Isaac’s has Jacob, and Jacob’s has Joseph, which he takes to answer why there is none of Abraham or of Joseph. Külling holds that the formulas are “the very fabric around which the whole of Genesis has been constructed”, not added later, against Wellhausen and Budde, who took them for the late scheme of a priestly source.
W. H. Gispen (1966) and Woudstra himself, who calls the approach “a fruitful one”, follow it. Wiseman (1936) reads the same formulas as closing their sections instead.
readings.note: Woudstra gives the sections’ verses from 5:1 on, except that Terah’s runs to Ishmael’s at 25:12; 1:1–2:3 stands before the first formula, and the first section runs to 5:1.

title: The shape of Leviticus
summary: Outlines of Leviticus differ over what holds it together. Driver sets chapters 17–26 apart as an older code built into the book, which Klostermann named the Law of Holiness; BibleProject reads the whole book as a mirror round the Day of Atonement. The words “This is the law of …” head the laws of chapters 6–7 and close those of 11–15. Two outlines are drawn here on the same verses, in the order they were proposed.

sources.title: An Introduction to the Literature of the Old Testament
sources.author: S. R. Driver
sources.note: pp. 39–55, on Leviticus

markers.label: “This is the law of …”
markers.summary: Thirteen verses of Leviticus have zōʾt tôrat (“this is the law of”). In chapters 6–7 the words open the laws of five offerings and sum them up at 7:37; in chapters 11–15 they come at or near the end of the laws of clean animals, childbirth, mildew, skin disease and discharges. No other verse of the book has them; 14:2 has “This shall be the law of”, with a verb between the two words.

readings.label: Priestly laws with the Law of Holiness set in
readings.summary: Driver reads Leviticus as part of the Priests’ Code “throughout”, in which “c. 17—26 constitute a section marked by certain special features of its own, and standing apart from the rest of the book”: laws of sacrifice, purification and atonement (1–16), the Law of Holiness (17–26), and a chapter on vows and tithes (27).
body: He holds that “an independent—and in all probability an older—body of priestly legislation lies at the basis of c. 17—26”, set apart by its phrasing, by holiness as “the leading motive of the entire section”, by laws repeated from elsewhere, and by opening with the place of sacrifice and closing with an exhortation, as the Book of the Covenant and Deuteronomy’s code do. The name “Das Heiligkeitsgesetz”, the Law of Holiness, he credits to Klostermann in 1877.

Within 1–16 he reads 6:8–7:38 as an “independent collection of laws linked together by the same formula”, “This is the law of …”, and chapters 11–15 as “linked together by the recurring colophon” of the same words.
readings.note: Driver numbers by the English verses, as the BSB does (6:1-7 are 5:20-26 in the Hebrew). The headings are his.

readings.label: A mirror round the Day of Atonement
readings.summary: BibleProject’s guide describes “an amazing symmetrical literary design”: rituals in the outer sections (1–7 and 23–25), the priests in the next (8–10 and 21–22), purity in “two matching sections” (11–15 and 18–20), and “At the center of the book (Lev. 16-17) is a key ritual, the Day of Atonement, that brings all the themes of the book together.”

title: The shape of Jonah
summary: Jonah is two journeys told in the same words: twice “the word of the LORD came to Jonah” (1:1, 3:1), and twice Jonah prays to the LORD (2:1, 4:2). BibleProject pairs the chapters on these lines; Bewer reads the book as one story into which the psalm of chapter 2 was later set. Two outlines are drawn here on the same verses, in the order they were proposed.

markers.label: “Jonah prayed to the LORD”
markers.summary: The verb wayyitpallēl (“and he prayed”) comes twice in Jonah: from inside the fish (2:1), followed by the psalm of 2:2-9, and after Nineveh is spared (4:2), when Jonah says he fled because he knew God to be “gracious and compassionate”.

readings.label: One story, with a psalm set into it
readings.summary: Bewer concludes “that the book is a unity, with the exception of the psalm” (2:2-9), with a few glosses. The psalm “is a psalm of thanksgiving for help received in great danger, not a prayer for help in the midst of danger”, so “this cannot be the prayer which Jonah prayed” inside the fish.
body: Of two possibilities, that the author chose the psalm or that a reader added it, Bewer holds the second “on the whole the more probable”: a reader who missed a thanksgiving after Jonah was thrown up on the shore wrote the psalm in the margin, meaning it to follow 2:10, and it was copied in after 2:1 instead. He dates it after the exile from its parallels with postexilic psalms.

He reports Sievers (1905) also taking the story as a unity except for the psalm, and rejects the proposals that divide the book into sources or rearrange it, Winckler’s, Erbt’s and Riessler’s among them: “all theories that work with several sources, or with many transpositions, are too artificial to be true.”
readings.note: Bewer numbers the psalm 2:3-10 in the Hebrew, 2:2-9 in English, as the BSB does. The section names are descriptive; his division is the psalm’s.

title: The shape of Matthew
summary: Matthew repeats two sets of words at a few points: five times “When Jesus had finished” after a long speech of Jesus, and twice “From that time on Jesus began”. Outlines of the book are built on one or the other, and Weren (2006) opens his survey of them: “The results of studies of this issue vary considerably.”. Five outlines are drawn here on the same verses, in the order they were proposed.

sources.title: ‘The Macrostructure of Matthew’s Gospel: A New Proposal’
sources.author: Wim J. C. Weren
sources.note: Biblica 87, pp. 171–200; a survey of the proposals, p. 171

markers.label: “When Jesus had finished …”
markers.summary: Five verses open with the same Greek words, καὶ ἐγένετο ὅτε ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (“and it came to pass when Jesus had finished”), and no other verse of Matthew does. Each follows a long speech of Jesus: the Sermon on the Mount, the sending of the twelve, the parables, the teaching on forgiveness among the disciples, and the woes and the end of the age.

markers.label: “From that time on …”
markers.summary: Matthew 4:17 and 16:21 open with the same Greek words, ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς (“from that time Jesus began”), the first followed by “to preach”, the second by “to show His disciples” that he must suffer. Weren notes that ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο occurs nowhere else in the New Testament or the Septuagint. ἀπὸ τότε alone stands once more, at 26:16, of Judas.

readings.label: Five books
readings.summary: Bacon divides Matthew into a preamble, five “books” and an epilogue. Each book is a narrative followed by a discourse and closed by the formula “when Jesus had finished”, which he compares to the five books of Moses, “each body of law introduced by a narrative of considerable length”.
body: Bacon reads the formula as the end of each book, and Matthew 1–2 and 26–28 as standing outside the five. He reports the five-fold division as “no recent discovery”, recognised by critics “a half-century ago”.

Weren reports that R. E. Brown largely follows Bacon, and that C. R. Smith (1997) argues for the five books from the alternation of narrative and discourse. Against Bacon, Weren cites Rolland, Barr and Luz, who read the formula as linking a discourse to what follows rather than closing it, and himself calls the placing of 26–28 outside the books “hardly convincing, since these chapters are indisputably the dramatic climax”.
readings.note: Bacon closes each book with its formula (7:28-29, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1a, 26:1), drawn here with the discourse it closes; 19:1b and 26:2, which the verse numbers join to it, go with it too. The verse boundaries are those Weren tabulates from Bacon; Bacon’s own contents give the same divisions by chapter.

readings.label: A mirror round the parables
readings.summary: Lohr counts the whole book, beginning and end included, as six narratives and five sermons in turn, and pairs them from the outside in, so that the parables of chapter 13 stand at the centre.
body: In Weren’s account, Lohr takes Matthew 23–25 as one discourse and treats 1–2 and 26–28 as narratives like the rest, so that the alternation runs through the whole book rather than only 3–25. H. J. B. Combrink proposes another concentric outline, also centred on chapter 13, whose segments differ from Lohr’s mainly in the three after the centre.

Weren answers the alternation readings as a group: the boundaries between narrative and discourse are not agreed (chapter 23 is a discourse to one author and a narrative to another), and the narrative sections contain long speeches of Jesus.
readings.note: Weren gives Lohr’s outline by chapters only.

readings.label: Three parts
readings.summary: Krentz, followed by Kingsbury and Bauer, divides Matthew in three at the two verses that open “From that time on Jesus began”: who Jesus is (1:1–4:16), his proclamation (4:17–16:20), and his journey to Jerusalem, suffering, death and resurrection (16:21–28:20).
body: On this reading each part has a caption (1:1, 4:17, 16:21) whose content the part goes on to elaborate, and the formula after the five discourses links rather than divides. Kingsbury, in Matthew as Story, divides the second and third parts in two again, at 11:2 and 26:1. Weren reports Gnilka’s commentary dividing at the same verses.

F. Neirynck, as Weren reports him, grants the parallel between 4:17 and 16:21 but reads each ἀπὸ τότε as tied to what comes just before it, as at 26:16, where it closes Judas’s bargain. Weren adds that the summaries recapitulating 4:17 stop at 11:1, and that “It is astonishing that this division into three is still so popular”.

readings.label: Hinges
readings.summary: Weren reads Matthew as a story that flows without deep breaks, held together by five “hinge texts” that each look back on the block before and open the one after: 4:12-17, 11:2-30, 16:13-28, 21:1-17 and 26:1-16.
body: He builds the outline from the story’s settings in time and place. A refrain of Jesus withdrawing (ἀνεχώρησεν), first noted by F. Breukelman, carries him away from Jerusalem and Judea up to 16:12; from 16:21 the passion predictions carry him towards it. Following Neirynck, he takes the three passages with ἀπὸ τότε (4:17, 16:21, 26:16) as opening new phases, and the hinge texts as Matera’s and Carter’s “kernels”.
Weren argues that earlier outlines differ so much because “Too much attention has been paid to rigid caesuras”, where in Matthew “The various sections of the book partly overlap”.

title: The shape of Mark
summary: Mark moves from Galilee to Jerusalem, and outlines of it differ over where the turn comes: at Jesus’ question near Caesarea Philippi (8:27), or when Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea (10:1). Three times on the way Jesus tells his disciples that the Son of Man will be killed and rise after three days. Three outlines are drawn here on the same verses, in the order they were proposed.

sources.author: H. B. Swete
sources.note: Introduction, pp. li–liv

markers.label: “After three days He will rise”
markers.summary: Three times between Caesarea Philippi and Jerusalem Jesus tells his disciples that the Son of Man will be killed and “after three days” rise: at 8:31, 9:31 and 10:33-34. Each time the narrative goes on to the disciples’ response: Peter rebukes him (8:32), they do not understand and argue over who is greatest (9:32-34), and James and John ask for the places at his right and left (10:35-37).

readings.label: Galilee and Jerusalem, with a bridge
readings.summary: Swete finds that “the book deals with two great themes, the Ministry in Galilee (i. 14—ix. 50), and the Last Week at Jerusalem (xi. 1—xvi. 8), and that these sections are connected by a comparatively brief survey of the period which intervened (x. 1—52).”
body: “The first fourteen verses of the Gospel are evidently introductory; the last twelve have the character of an appendix, which links the Gospel history with the fortunes of the Church in the Apostolic age.” Within the Galilean ministry he traces a plan: the lakeside towns, the rest of Galilee during withdrawals from the lake, and the training of the Twelve.
On this outline the turn at Caesarea Philippi falls inside the Galilean ministry, which runs on to 9:50; Bacon (1909) divides there instead.
readings.note: Swete calls the first fourteen verses introductory but begins the ministry in Galilee at 1:14; 1:14 is drawn with the ministry.

readings.label: Two parts of three divisions
readings.summary: Bacon finds that “the narrative falls into two parts of nearly equal extent”: the Galilean Ministry (1:1–8:26) and the Judaean Ministry (8:27–16:8), each in three divisions. “Like the book of Acts the Gospel of Mark thus falls into two Parts of three Divisions each.”
body: He holds that the divisions’ limits “are so clearly defined by the subject matter that all interpreters are in substantial agreement as to their extent”, the one doubt being where the fourth ends: the healing of Bartimaeus (10:46-52) is “an epilogue forming a transition to the next Division, with which some excellent authorities have grouped it”. He follows Matthew in marking the transition at 11:1.
Swete (1898), before him, runs the Galilean ministry on to 9:50.
readings.note: The headings are Bacon’s. He ends the Gospel at 16:8 and calls 16:9-20 an epilogue, “Shorter and Longer Ending”.

readings.label: A drama in three acts
readings.summary: BibleProject’s guide reads Mark as “a drama with three acts. The first act is set in Galilee, the second act is Jesus traveling, and the third takes place in Jerusalem.” In Act 1 “everyone is amazed and wondering who Jesus is”, in Act 2 “the disciples struggle to understand what it means for Jesus to be the Messiah”, and in Act 3 “we see the paradoxical way Jesus becomes the messianic King”.
body: Its poster sets three conversations in Act 2 (8:27-38, 9:30-37, 10:32-45), and the guide ends the book at 16:8, “with Jesus’ disciples showing the same kind of fear and confusion that concluded the first two acts”. It describes 16:9-20 as a longer ending “only found in later, less reliable manuscripts”.
readings.note: The act boundaries are those of the guide’s contents (1:1-8:26, 8:27-10, 11-16, and 16:9-20).
